newsitem.title: PERU: Rescue strike leaves MRTA spent force-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Rescue strike leaves MRTA spent force-analysts.

text.p: Peru's dramatic hostage rescue has dealt a devastating blow to the Tupac Amaru guerrillas, a fading rebel group whose desperate attempt to resuscitate itself has backfired disastrously, analysts said on Wednesday.
But they said the Marxist Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) will not vanish despite the failure of its bid to grab influence by holding 72 VIPs hostage since Dec. 17.

"I think it is horrendous for the movement. It now means the MRTA is a spent force," David Scott Palmer, a leading author on Peruvian guerrillas, told Reuters by telephone from Boston. "But there will be some sympathy for the perceived heroic action. They will not go away completely. They have come back several times."

As the bodies of the 14 hostage-takers, many in their teens, lay in the burned-out mansion, leading Peruvian guerrilla analyst Carlos Tapia said the MRTA would not easily recover from its "suicide attack."
"I do not think the MRTA, at least not in the short-term, will be able to rebuild itself," he told local Radioprograms.
But the MRTA, whose armed members are estimated to number fewer than 200, responded with threats of further attacks and defiant statements that the 15-year-old group would carry on.

"We are not afraid that our comrades have died. The MRTA is not going to die," an MRTA rebel in Lima told Reuters. The rebel said the group would "take a breather" due to increased government security measures but it would "reorientate" its leadership and make "specific attacks" to avenge the deaths of its members and leader Nestor Cerpa on Tuesday.
MRTA international spokesman Isaac Velazco said the group had long planned to strike at military and economic tragets in response to an assault on the residence.

"The MRTA has lost most of its operational capacity. But they do have some forces left in the jungle. It is possible that within the next three months they might try to mount some desperate operation," Scott Palmer said.

Even Peru's triumphant President Alberto Fujimori, basking in the victorious end to the toughest crisis of his career, was careful to avoid appearing over-confident. "It could be that it (terrorism) is not defeated", he said, adding that the armed forces, which had tightened security at diplomatic sites around Lima, were prepared to counter any reprisal attacks.

The MRTA's military leader in the central jungle, where the group has its only permanent armed presence, told Reuters before Tuesday's rescue operation that Cerpa had chosen his own successor before the siege.

But Nelson Manrique, a Peruvian historian, agreed with police reports that the group was left without a genuine leader and would need time to restructure, just as it did after the 1992 capture of MRTA leader Victor Polay brought the group to its knees. Only a slow reorganization allowed it to rebuild sufficiently to attempt spectacular one-off strikes like the Dec. 17 storming of the Japanese compound.
"The MRTA is again left without political direction. Nestor Cerpa was the only political leader and those remaining have little experience," Manrique said.

In the medium-term, however, the MRTA could get a boost if sympathy for the hostage-takers takes root among students and swells the ranks of a group that recruits its fighters as young as 12, Scott Palmer said.

Analysts said the group started off in the mid-1980s as a Robin Hood-style band robbing trucks to distribute food to the poor, but it quickly lost sympathy with its increasingly bloody bombing and kidnapping campaigns.
"If we do not achieve social justice and build real peace, who can say that there will not be youngsters waiting to follow in Cerpa's footsteps?" Tapia asked.

But the more immediate threat to peace in Peru, where 17 years of guerrilla wars have cost 30,000 lives and $25 billion in infrastructure damage, comes from the Shining Path -- the country's much larger and bloodier rebel group.

"The Shining Path has been taking advantage of the government's distraction at the residence. It will continue to do grassroot organising and will attack police posts and kill local officials," Scott Palmer predicted.

That fear was not far from the mind of Lima taxi-driver Victor Montalvo Crena, 66. "If the government says terrorism is over, that's wrong," he said. "The groups' numbers have been reduced but there are still members and we cannot afford to lower our guard."
